# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 64 — The EMET Bible (Literal)

**Translator:** EMET | **Source:** P.Mich. 130, Shepherd of Hermas 64 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_064_page_001.jpg

---

## Similitude 6, Part 2 — The Shepherd of Luxury and Deception

**64:1** He showed me two shepherds. And one of them was dressed in beautiful clothing and had a white complexion and a handsome body, and the other one was thin with a dark complexion, and he wore rough clothing and grievous appearance. He said to me: "Do you see these shepherds?"

**64:2** "I see them, lord," I said. "The fine one," he said, "is the angel of luxury and deception. He destroys the souls of the servants of God and turns them away from truth, beguiling them with evil desires in which they shall perish. For they forget the commandments of the living God and walk in vain deceptions and arrogances of this life, and they are destroyed by this angel — some unto death, and some unto the corruption of their lives."

**64:3** "I said to him: Lord, I do not know how this angel of luxury destroys the souls of men." "Listen," he said. "When a desire comes upon any of the servants of God to live in luxury or deceit, and this man places before himself vain and empty desires, this angel of deception who is with him fills the man's heart with great desires, implanting vain pleasures — and that man seems to himself to be doing good, while in fact doing evil. When therefore he is satisfied, he is filled with great blindness for what he has done."

**64:4** "Lord," I said, "I do not understand these things about the angel of luxury." "Listen further," he said. "Of all the deeds which a man does in his life, certain deeds seem to be righteous, but in the sight of the Lord they are sins. Thus the man who thinks that he has done good — he has done nothing righteous for the Lord. And thus every sin appears as something sweet and pleasurable in the life of this world, with the result that the servants of God are corrupted."

---

*EMET renders the Greek of P.Mich. 130 with maximal literalness, preserving the Two Shepherds vision at the opening of Similitude 6.*
